courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Greek Drama from Page to Stage
courses.description: This seminar takes a participatory approach to ancient Greek theater, exploring the dual nature of drama as performance and script. It provides a historical overview of the extraordinary Athenian fifth century (BCE), emphasizing ways theater interacts with art, law, myth, and politics. Theatrical exercises and performances complement several writing assignments. Honors version available.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Three Greek and Roman Epics
courses.description: This first-year seminar will involve a close reading of Homer's Iliad and Odyssey and Vergil's Aeneid, and as a transition from Homer to Vergil, students will also read the tragedies of Sophocles from fifth-century Athens. Honors version available.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Dead and Deadly Women: Greek Tragic Heroines from Aeschylus to Eliot
courses.description: This seminar will study the great tragic heroines of ancient Greek drama, focusing on Clytemnestra, Medea, Alcestis, Phaedra, the Trojan Women, Antigone. Students will also read a contemporary novel, by Fay Weldon, that engages many of these mythic women. Students will study the Greek tragedies intensively, along with their reception in later literature and art. Honors version available.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Ancient Magic and Religion
courses.description: In this class, we examine descriptions of religious and magical practices in the multicultural contexts of ancient Greece and Rome. Our sources include literary accounts, legal documents, and material objects, such as inscriptions, amulets, tablets, magical images, and papyri.

source.text: CLAS 59. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-CREATE or FC-GLOBAL.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Writing the Past
courses.description: Translated works of three Greek historians--Herodotus, Thucydides, and Polybius--will provide a lens through which to explore the capacity for literature and other modes of representation to convey history. Honors version available.

source.text: CLAS 61. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-KNOWING or FC-PAST.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Bandits, Barbarians, and Rebels in the Ancient Mediterranean
courses.description: A study of Greek and Roman depictions of marginalized and peripheral peoples in both literary and visual sources, with consideration of the origin, development, and social roles ascribed to these groups.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: The Politics of Persuasion in the Ancient and Modern Worlds
courses.description: Are there rules for crafting a successful speech? The art and the mechanisms of persuasion will be considered both as a discipline with its own laws and practices and as a window into the values and debates that animate the public life of diverse civilizations. Honors version available.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Cinema and the Ancient World
courses.description: In this first-year seminar, students will investigate what films set in classical Roman antiquity say about contemporary culture, and will also attempt to understand their impact on the shaping of our sense of history.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: The City of Rome
courses.description: This first-year seminar is an introduction to the history and art of Rome from antiquity through the present. Students will survey the entire period, but will look in particular at four specific periods in the city's life from the early second century CE until the present day. Honors version available.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Helen of Troy: From Homer to Hollywood
courses.description: The myth of Helen of Troy has inspired countless creative responses, from Homer's Iliad to Hollywood's Troy; all of them raise questions about the value of beauty and love within society. The course requires no prior knowledge of the classics, although you should be familiar with Homer's Iliad and Odyssey.

source.text: CLAS 67. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-AESTH or FC-KNOWING.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Special Topics
courses.description: Special topics course; contents will vary each semester. Honors version available.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: The Greeks
courses.description: Introduction to the history, literature, religion, philosophy, science, art and architecture of Greece from Homer to Alexander the Great. Emphasis on primary sources. Honors version available.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: The Romans
courses.description: A survey of Roman civilization from the beginning to the late empire, dealing with history, literature, art and architecture, philosophy and religion, and social and political institutions. Honors version available.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Summer Study Abroad in Greece
courses.description: Introduction to the history and culture of ancient Greece, from the Bronze Age to the end of the Roman period, through field study of historical and archaeological sites in Greece.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Medical Word Formation and Etymology
courses.description: Systematic study of the formation of medical terms from Greek and Latin roots, to build vocabulary and recognition. For general etymology see CLAS 125.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Classical Mythology
courses.description: An introduction to the mythology of the ancient Greek and Roman world. Readings may include selections from Homer, Hesiod, Greek tragedy, and Vergil. Honors version available.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Epic and Tragedy
courses.description: Study of classical epic and tragedy. Special emphasis on Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, and on the rethinking of Homeric epic in the tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: The Theater in the Greek and Roman World
courses.description: An investigation of the history, aesthetics, politics, and influence of theater in the ancient Greek and Roman world, with attention to themes of power, passion, rhetoric, resistance, gender, and identity. The course also includes a substantial practical component, with students taking on a number of the dramaturgical roles involved in the production of ancient drama. Honors version available.

source.text: CLAS 231. | 3 Credits. | FC-CREATE or FC-POWER, COMMBEYOND.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Roman Wisdom
courses.description: A survey of the major philosophical of the Roman world, from the Republic to the empire, including Stoicism, Epicureanism, Skepticism, Platonism, and their relationship to Christianity.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Women in Greek Art and Literature
courses.description: Course examines law, religion, medicine, social practices, and ideologies in the lives of women in ancient Greece, from Homer to Hellenistic Egypt, using literature, art, and epigraphy. Honors version available.

source.text: CLAS 240. | 3 Credits. | FC-AESTH or FC-KNOWING. | WGST 240 .

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Women in Ancient Rome
courses.description: Course examines the life of women in ancient Rome, from the first beginnings of the organized community in Rome through the early Empire, a period of about 900 years. Also explores aspects of the lives of women in provinces governed by Rome. Honors version available.

source.text: CLAS 241. | 3 Credits. | FC-KNOWING or FC-PAST. | WGST 241 .

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Sex and Gender in Antiquity
courses.description: Exploration of gender constructs, what it meant to be a woman or a man, in antiquity, as revealed in literary, historical, and archaeological sources. Readings from Homer, Euripides, Plato, Ovid, Virgil, Juvenal, Petronius, and other ancient authors.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Race and Ethnicity in the Ancient Mediterranean
courses.description: This course examines constructions of race and ethnicity in the ancient Mediterranean through art, literature, and archaeology. Students gain a background in the history and culture of the classical world that grounds critical analysis of the primary source evidence, both textual and material. By engaging with modern scholarship on ancient ideas about race and ethnic identity, students also learn to evaluate and critique secondary source material in their original contexts.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Pericles and Athens
courses.description: An introduction to classical civilization through study of its most important period in Greece. Attention to history, philosophy, and art. Lecture and discussion. Honors version available.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Alexander and the Hellenistic World
courses.description: An introduction to Greek civilization through study of the period in which it spreads beyond mainland Greece to influence and partially merge with the cultures of the Near East, Egypt, and Rome. Attention to history, literature, philosophy, and art. Lectures and discussion.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Augustus and Rome
courses.description: An introduction to classical civilization through study of the literature, history, and art of one of the most crucial periods in Roman history. Lectures and discussion. Honors version available.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: The Early Roman Empire
courses.description: An introduction to the civilization of the Roman Empire through study of the literature, history, and archaeology of its most colorful period.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Pagans and Christians
courses.description: Pagans and Christians in the Roman Empire. Special attention to the fundamental cultural and social changes resulting from the Christianization of the Empire. Honors version available.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Ancient Medicine
courses.description: Study of medicine in the ancient Mediterranean world focusing on Greek and Roman understandings of the body, medical theories, and health-care practices. Consideration of medicine and healing traditions as culturally embedded practices using literary and archaeological sources. Honors version available.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Ancient Magic & Religion
courses.description: This course examines the roles and technologies of magic and religion in the ancient Greek and Roman worlds, paying special attention to their local contexts and to the myths and actual techniques ancient practitioners used to serve their clientele. Students analyze descriptions in literary and legal documents and also material objects, such as inscriptions, amulets, tablets, magical images, and papyri. This course is a "maker" course, with a significant amount of time spent in the BeAM Makerspace to work on assignments.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Athletics in the Greek and Roman Worlds
courses.description: Study of athletics as a unifying force in ancient society, emphasizing the Olympic games and other religious festivals. Consideration of athletic professionalism, propaganda, and social trends using literary and archaeological sources. Honors version available.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Classics and Cinema
courses.description: From the sword-and-sandal spectacles of Hollywood's golden age to contemporary art films that whisper rather than roar, cinema has maintained an evolving, almost obsessive conversation with classical antiquity. This course explores how filmmakers have reimagined, interrogated, and sometimes reinvented Greece and Rome, examining not only historical epics and mythological adaptations but also films that transpose ancient narratives into radically different contexts.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Classical Rhetoric and American Democracy
courses.description: This course introduces students to the complex role of rhetoric and speechmaking in the American democracy and its two most important predecessors, the Athenian democracy of the fifth and fourth centuries BCE and the Roman republic of the fourth through the first century BCE. Students will learn about foundational documents and key milestones of the democratic experience in America alongside documents from ancient Greece and Rome. In many cases, we will be reading the very texts that influenced the founding fathers, Abraham Lincoln, Martin Luther King, Jr., John F. Kennedy, and other American leaders.

source.text: CLAS 271. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-VALUES, FAD.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Classical Rhetoric: The Science of Persuasive Speech in Classical Antiquity and Beyond
courses.description: This course focuses on Ancient Greek and Roman rhetoric and their global legacies. Students will explore the representation of persuasive speech; engage and analyze ancient theories of rhetoric and explore how these have influenced communication around the world. Students will also practice their own rhetorical and oratorical skills.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Globalizing the Classics
courses.description: Study the rewriting and re-imagining of ancient Greek and Roman civilizations - their literature, art, and other cultural products - in a geographically and temporally global context.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Homer and the Heroic Age of Greece
courses.description: Homer's Iliad and Odyssey and modern interpretations of Homer in text and film.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Greek Tragedy
courses.description: An introduction to the three great tragedians of ancient Greece and to their historical and cultural context. Discussion is based on close readings of the English translations of selected plays by Aeschylus, Euripides, and Sophocles. Honors version available.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Latin and Greek Lyric Poetry in Translation
courses.description: Introduction to the lyric and elegiac poetry of antiquity in English translation, including Hesiod, Sappho, Catullus, Ovid, and Horace. Honors version available.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: The Classical Background of English Poetry
courses.description: Study of classical writers' influence on selected genres of English poetry. Honors version available.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: The Lives of Others from Herodotus to Tacitus
courses.description: Explores ethnographic writing in the Ancient Mediterranean. How did the Greeks and Romans write about Persians, Egyptians, Scythians, Gauls, Germans, Britons, Hyperboreans, Spartans, and other peoples across time? In what ways did they understand their own identities and explain the distinctions they perceived between other peoples? The course will include some comparison of modern conceptions of ethnicity and depictions of group identities (in film, literature, and other media).

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Love and Death, Fantasy and Magic: The Greek and Roman Novel
courses.description: Star-crossed lovers, pirates, magic, show trials, faked deaths, talking animals, exotic lands, fantastic machines, and happy endings. All these and more characterize the most sensational genre of ancient literature, the prose fiction that was composed in Greek and Latin in the first few centuries CE. Scholars often call these works "ancient novels," and they have been read enthusiastically from antiquity until today. In this class, we will consider the historical and social context of the novels and will learn to interpret and critique them with regard to narrative, style, rhetoric, and characterization.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Cicero, Caesar, and the End of the Roman Republic
courses.description: This course examines the lives, works, and impact of Julius Caesar and Cicero during the tumultuous final years of the Roman Republic. It explores their political careers, literary achievements, and conflicting ideologies through an interdisciplinary lens. Students analyze primary texts, archaeological evidence, and various historical methodologies to understand these figures' roles in the Republic's downfall and the rise of the principate. The course emphasizes social inequality, cultural change, and the application of power in Roman society. It provides a comprehensive view of this pivotal period in Roman history, encouraging students to apply diverse research approaches to historical analysis.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Emperors, Tyrants, Kings, and Rulers in Ancient Greece and Rome
courses.description: Pericles built an empire; Caligula thought he was a god; Nero fiddled while Rome burned; and Commodus dressed as a gladiator and fought in the arena. The history of Greece and Rome is full of scandalous stories about eccentric and even insane leaders (and their wives) whose reigns raise questions about the nature of power and a ruler's role in administering the empire. In this course, we will look at accounts of leaders and forms of government in ancient sources and trace their impact on the founding documents of America.

source.text: CLAS 380. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-POWER, FAD.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Junior Seminar
courses.description: The topic of this course varies according to instructor, but in all cases is designed to bring together all departmental majors in their examination of a particular topic in the study of the ancient Mediterranean from an interdisciplinary perspective. Seminar format and research focus. Majors only, junior or senior standing required.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Independent Research in Classics
courses.description: This course allows a student to design and execute an independent research project under the supervision of a faculty member. Although the specifics will be determined on a case-by-case basis by the student and the faculty supervisor, the project will normally involve the careful study of key primary sources and engagement with relevant scholarship, and culminate in a major research paper (around 25 pages) or a suitable equivalent in another format (e.g., website, video). Permission of the Instructor.
courses.repeat_rules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Independent Study in Classical Studies
courses.description: Students may suggest to the chair of the department topics for individual or group study. Advance arrangements required.
courses.repeat_rules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Greek and Roman Historians
courses.description: The study in English translation of selections from Herodotus, Thucydides, Livy, Tacitus, and others, with consideration of their literary qualities and their readability as historians. Honors version available.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Ancient Greco-Roman Medicine and Philosophy
courses.description: This cross-listed course offers a high-level coverage of central texts in Ancient Greco-Roman Medicine with the aim of providing students with a thorough understanding of the philosophical foundations of Western medicine.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Roman Law
courses.description: This course combines a survey of the main areas of Roman law in their social and historical context with the close study of primary texts illustrating Roman law in practice, especially case studies from the writings of Roman legal experts; particular attention is given to the logic and application of ancient Roman legal thought and to its social and ethical implications. Honors version available.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Grammar as a Guide to Effective Writing
courses.description: A systematic review of English grammar for students of Latin and Greek, combined with practical exercises in prose style and effective writing.

source.text: CLAS 511. | 1 Credits. | Prerequisite, GREK 204 or LATN 204 .

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Honors Course
courses.description: Honors course for departmental majors in classical archaeology, classical civilization, Greek, and Latin.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Honors Course
courses.description: Honors course for departmental majors in classical archaeology, classical civilization, Greek, and Latin.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Proseminar in Pedagogy
courses.description: This course is an introduction to the issues, skills, and resources relevant to the successful teaching of undergraduate courses in Classics Departments at post-secondary educational institutions.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Proseminar in Professional Development
courses.description: This course is an introduction to skills and practices that play a key part in the professional lives of classicists and classical archaeologists working in post-secondary educational institutions.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Methods, Resources, and Perspectives in Classical Scholarship for Graduate Students
courses.description: This course is a requirement for the M.A. in Classics. The goal of the course is to provide pre-M.A. students with an overview of the field and of its development; and to provide them with resources and methods that will help them to conduct their own research in an informed fashion. Graduate students only.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Approaches to Women in Antiquity
courses.description: Intensive interdisciplinary introduction to women in antiquity, using literary, historical, and visual materials. Open to senior classics majors by permission of the instructor.

courses.subject: CLAS
courses.title: Seminars in Classical Studies
courses.description: Graduate research seminar. Topics vary from year to year. Graduate standing.
